sm: This episode of The District Club reviews the midterm elections, where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and won Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Maine and both Carolinas. James Talarico became the first Democrat to win statewide in Texas in 32 years, and Susan Collins lost her seat. Mike Johnson is stepping aside as Speaker, setting up a Scalise versus Jordan contest, and the Alaska Senate race is down to a few hundred votes. Ben says every Republican faction lost and warns about Texas, where Democrats also flipped the state house and supreme court. Tim calls it a vote against Republicans, and blames the White House for having no message on the Iran war.

Tim argues the president should have asked for national sacrifice over the Iran war, which would have let Republicans run on it or distance themselves without a full break. Isabelle says she was not shocked, and points to Congressman Brandon Gill, who won his Texas district by 11 points where Talarico later won by over 10, as the one clear Republican winner. She says voters want bold, unapologetic new leadership. Mary Margaret reports that White House staffers privately blamed the Iran war and affordability. Ben pushes back, noting the president's approval was 40 percent before the war and 37 percent on election day, so Iran made existing problems worse. He adds that Republicans had no consistent message on data centers or affordability.

The panel discusses affordability and young voters. Isabelle says young men swung most against the administration, citing the 50-year mortgage idea, a Republican amnesty bill, and messaging that scolded young people. Tim says Democrats' answer of give it away free is gaining ground on issues like affordability. Mary Margaret says candidates needed an honest conversation about the war's effect on gas prices, and that young men remain hung up on Epstein and conspiracy theories. Ben says Democrats turned Epstein into shorthand for corruption, and that Republicans failed to message on corruption and government waste even in the first major election since DOGE.

Isabelle notes that conservative ballot measures passed even in deep blue states. Colorado banned boys in girls sports, banned child gender transition procedures, and imposed life without parole for child sex trafficking. Voter ID and citizenship requirements passed in blue states, Idaho defeated an abortion measure, and California is likely to reject a billionaire tax. North Carolina rejected two taxes and strengthened voter ID. She blames DC consultants for telling candidates to avoid culture war issues, citing Mike Rogers and Michelle Steel's softening on abortion. Mary Margaret recalls a Jim Banks memo urging Republicans to lean into culture wars. Tim says the party can't win by being based and redpilled alone, and must act more like a political party with hard policy alternatives.

Tim says the White House has memes but no healthcare plan. Mary Margaret asks about a possible immigration deal with the new Democratic majority. Tim is open to it if it doesn't bring back DACA. Isabelle strongly disagrees, calling the pullback from mass deportations a mistake, and notes that rents fell in cities with many deportations, such as New Orleans, Nashville and Texas cities. She describes an ICE ride-along where a suburban woman refused to help find a convicted sexual predator. Mary Margaret says deportations succeeded faster than expected, which frightened some Republicans into backing off, and suggests the president could talk with congressional leaders about the next phase without compromising.

Isabelle argues Republicans keep compromising out of fear of nonexistent middle voters. She cites the Mike Rogers and Michelle Steel ads, and Vivek Ramaswamy's H-1B promise. She says candidate quality must change, with candidates willing to say the hard thing, and contrasts Gill's win with Talarico's. Mary Margaret mentions Michael Alfonso, a young conservative who won in Wisconsin, and criticizes Rogers's abortion statement. Ben says immigration is a test of whether Republicans will defend their policies, as they defended the unpopular war. He then says Ted Cruz should drop presidential plans and save Texas, and that Kevin McCarthy should run the RNC.

The group turns to JD Vance's post blaming the Iran war for the losses. Ben calls it a huge mistake and a sign of weakness that signals separation from Trump. Mary Margaret says Vance's lukewarm view of the war was known and that he stayed loyal. Tim says it likely lowered the chance of a Trump endorsement, which is Vance's best path to the presidency. Isabelle says Vance wrote that the president agreed, and for many it was cathartic. Ben says Vance is the least popular vice president in modern history, and that the post invited other contenders to enter. The panel disagrees on whether it damaged him.

The panel continues on Vance, with Tim saying he separated from Trump too early, and Mary Margaret saying the post came midday Wednesday, not minutes after polls closed. Isabelle says young white Gen Z men swung 38 points from Republicans to Democrats between 2024 and 2026, and that reaching them is essential for 2028. Ben notes most of them stayed home rather than switching. Isabelle says Republicans need a blueprint for the next generation's American dream, and Mary Margaret says young men feel promises such as no new wars were broken. Ben closes by noting the richest man in the world spent 200 million dollars in Texas with little effect, so Republicans must rethink how they communicate.
